screens.body: HTML and CSS build a beautiful statue — it just stands there. JavaScript brings it to life. JS is the scripting language of the browser: it reacts when users click, type, and scroll. Dropdown menus, form checks, live updates — that's all JavaScript. It runs right in the browser, no server needed.

options: Reacts to what the user does
check.question: JavaScript in the browser…

screens.heading: JavaScript makes pages respond
screens.keyPoint: JavaScript makes pages react to users.

screens.body: Variables hold data your script needs. Use let when the value will change (like a score), and const when it won't (like an app name). Giving values names means you can reuse them and your code reads like plain English. Pick names that say what the value is.
screens.heading: Variables hold data
screens.keyPoint: let for values that change, const for values that don't.

screens.body: The DOM is the browser's tree of your page (you met it in HTML Foundations). JavaScript can grab any element from that tree with document.querySelector — pass it a CSS selector, and it hands you the matching element. Once you have it, you can read it, change it, or listen to it.
screens.heading: Grabbing elements: the DOM
screens.keyPoint: querySelector grabs any element using a CSS selector.

screens.body: An event is something that happens: a click, a keypress, a page load. You tell an element to listen for an event with addEventListener, and hand it a function to run when the event fires. This pattern — 'when X happens, do Y' — is the heart of interactivity.

options: Something that happens, like a click
check.question: An event is…

screens.heading: Listening for events
screens.keyPoint: When X happens, do Y — that's event handling.

screens.body: Once you've grabbed an element, you can change it live. textContent swaps the text inside it; style tweaks its CSS. The page updates instantly, no reload needed. This is how like-buttons flip, counters tick up, and error messages appear next to forms.

check.question: To change what a heading says…

screens.heading: Changing the page live
screens.keyPoint: textContent and style update the page instantly.

screens.body: Scripts need to make decisions too. An if statement runs code only when its condition is true — like checking a password or an age. Comparison operators (>, <, ===) ask yes-or-no questions about your data. Logic in scripting is just decisions written down.
screens.heading: Logic: if statements
screens.keyPoint: if runs code only when its condition is true.

screens.body: Functions bundle actions under a name so you can reuse them. Define the steps once with function, then call it whenever — from a click listener, from another function, anywhere. Methods are just functions attached to objects, like console.log or addEventListener.

options: Bundles code you can run again and again
Is a kind of CSS class
check.question: A function…

screens.heading: Functions bundle actions
